selectedWork.title: Selected Work
selectedWork.introduction: These are some projects that I felt were worth cherry-picking and noting specifically. If you'd like to learn more about any of these projects, drop me a note!

projects.name: AI / LLM Registry
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, primary implementer, technical lead maintainer
projects.claim: A company-wide registry for versioned agent assets, built on the durable ideas behind npm and container registries.
projects.description: Architected, implemented, and delivered a vendor-neutral platform for distributing serializable large language model assets (Agents, Skills, Model Configs, MCP Support, etc.) with extensible cross harness support and integrations, with full-fledged support for semantic versioning, team-scoped namespaces, an localized history database model. A CAC-based bun CLI client exposes installation, discovery, submission, rollback, and a suite of roughly thirty other operations that support improved agentic development workflows.
evidence: Thousands of cataloged, published, and installed assets
Adopted company wide
SQLite-backed client history, dependency installation, rollback, and nightly releases
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, npm, CAC, SQLite, Rust, PostgreSQL

projects.name: Springfield
projects.context: Charter Communications · Principal architect, implementer, long-term owner
projects.claim: A deterministic software-intelligence platform that turns a massive system (65+) of distributed frontends into a queryable model of the system with extensive MCP integrations.
projects.description: I built Springfield end to end as a stateless ETL system. It clones source code MFE packages into a local temporary filesystem cache, crawls them in parallel, converts source code into ASTs, and runs ETL pipelines over the result, converting source code data into size optimized intermediary representative data files, and finally ingesting those data files into a series of databases. Those pipelines map cross-package imports and exports, catalog React components and hooks, reproduce component rendering, and trace downstream service and payload usage. The resulting data lakes are available through REST, GraphQL, MCP tools, and a conversational interface. Models can consume Springfield's facts. This has supported enhanced observability into the system, and worked to improve developer experience and starkly increase developer and product velocity in this distributed microfrontend model. I named it Springfield after the Simpsons, which I'm super into.
evidence: Complete end to end refresh in under four minutes with zero inference tokens (concurrent automomous, deterministic ETL pipelines)
Roughly 118,000 database writes in about 875 milliseconds
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Rust, AST analysis, ETL, GraphQL, REST, MCP

projects.name: Amazon Platform Engineering
projects.claim: Platform work spanning design systems, microfrontends, regulated payments, and production reliability.
projects.description: I founded and served as Technical Lead for Gotham Design System, a design system used across Prime Gaming, Prime Video, and digital-goods storefront experiences, offering extensive theming improvements and media immersification tooling over the standard AUI amazon ecommerce design system. I proposed, architected, implemented, and owned the migration of a massive monolithic digital goods next.js frontend toward distributed team level microfrontends with autonmous framework stacks, enabling autonomous decoupled releases, reducing builds from upwards of 11 minutes to under 2 minutes. I architected a solution for Digital Goods European payment and compliance requirements allowing European Users to have one-time checkout credit card use, and built high-availability synthetic monitoring (canaries) for critical digital goods checkout and digital fulfillment flows using cloudformation and cloudwatch. Served as Lead Frontend Engineer for Amazon Games research and development lab, Playmaker Labs, publishing highly gamified storefront experiences in conjunction with Prime Gaming, Luna, and Twitch. Architected migration of client side rendered Prime Gaming storefront to a server side rendered application, with lazy asset loading, improving initial page load times by 68%.
evidence: Shared interface foundations across multiple Amazon product organizations
Build time reduced from eleven minutes to six
Payment and compliance orchestration for European markets
Synthetic monitoring for high-availability customer experiences
projects.technologies: React, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, design systems, microfrontends,graphQL, AWS, distributed workflows

projects.name: Evergreen Terrace
projects.claim: A private scalable model for a lone engineer's gas-town.
projects.description: Gastown is an untenable model. Distributed work for people with bottomless pockets. Not what the average engineer needs. This is a service infrastructure for an autonomous agent work lifecycle system that accelerates a single developer, or a small team's, working velocity.
evidence: Persistent work and context across specialist agents
Operational dashboard and orchestration surfaces
Containerized for cross platform compatibility
projects.technologies: TypeScript, Bun, React, agent orchestration, MCP, SQLite

projects.name: Cross-session Context Store
projects.claim: Shared, durable engineering memory for Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro sessions.
projects.description: This one's pretty straight forward. If you've ever used AWS AgentCore Memory this is a private, open source, cross harness compatible version. Its just how you want memory in a harness to work: hands off, loaded on demand deterministically through standard harness lifecycle events, and nothing leaves your machine to feed the wet, slobbering mouth of big data.
evidence: FTS5 and BM25 retrieval over typed, scoped memories
Review queues, conflict handling, decay, and explicit handoffs
Cross-Harness Support (Claude, Kiro-*, Codex)
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, SQLite, FTS5, React, MCP

projects.name: Bit Context Protocol
projects.claim: A compact binary format for structured model context.
projects.description: This one's heavily based on some work I had done previously around ext4 filesystems. It's an approach to efficient context window delegation through a dumb byte container protocol medium. It's still in early workings, but the stable prerelease is available for use today in rust and typescript.
evidence: Binary (dumb container) protocol for efficient context management
projects.technologies: Binary protocols, TypeScript, schema design, fuzz testing, LLM context

projects.name: Bundt
projects.claim: A set of independently versioned developer tools built around Bun.
projects.description: Bundt is a system of bun developer tooling. This is to say, developer tooling, built with the same foundational bun toolchain and with a turborepo monorepo approach. Think oxc but with one ten millionth the funding. Not gonna lie, there's some bangers in this one. There's a performant language-agnostic react compiler and renderer (render your app in rust), there's a framework/harness for a server side rendered dynamic UI composition from a language model and component registry, there's a performant signals state library (framework agnostic), and some LLM developer tooling, amidst many other flavors of the weak.
evidence: Independent application and library release boundaries
Agent orchestration, documentation, SSR, and local-inference tooling
A practical proving ground for shared packages without forced coupling
projects.technologies: Bun, TypeScript, React, SSR, MCP, monorepo tooling

projects.name: Project Arcturus
projects.claim: A long-lived publishing system and the site you are using now.
projects.description: This is frameworkless, modern, organized, scalable, performant React. It is also the current site you are on! This is my website, project-arcturus, a custom framework-less bun prerendering and static site generation process. React Suspense in conjunction with Suspense Enabled Query Providers for instant data hydration with background refreshes. All the react you were promised and never got from that one guy.
evidence: Static publishing backed by a structured content pipeline
Progressive design-system, accessibility, and highly optimized framework-less prerendering pipeline
projects.technologies: React, TypeScript, Bun, SSR, prerendering, content pipelines, monorepo tooling

principles.title: How I Engineer
principles.introduction: These are some principles that I've come to value over my career, in regards to how we approach software as engineers:

items.title: Ownership
items.description: Ownership involves a model of what I'd call perpetual accountability, and an adaptive approach to software. Ownership is not inherently singular, but it involves a level of personal responsibility over software deployed by you and your team. In the 'pager' age, this meant an intricate understanding of the services under your purview. In the modern 'llm' age, this is being pushed more towards being able to produce a rapid understanding of software generated under your agent suite/fleet in the event of outages or long term maintenance needs. An agent cannot at this time own a service(s) infrastructure. Ownership is still a human quality.

items.title: Bias for Action
items.description: This comes down to being able to, in your software ecosystem, correctly identify one way and two way doors. A two-way door is a decision that is easy to reverse or do a different way, such as component development, or a service client implementation. These 'doors' do not require consensus for action, we expect that our engineers, through their experience and expertise, can move quickly through two way doors. A one way door, by contract, is an expensive decision that should require consensus and approval from the team before moving forward. An example of this would be choosing a cloud provider and migrating an on-premise infrastructure to it. It's important to get these right the first time. Bias for action means being someone that does not wait to deliver on two-way door work. It also means being able to identify what software needs, and doing it, not waiting for a Jira ticket.

items.title: Strong Opinions, Loosely Held
items.description: This one's simple: Have opinions. Ground them in data, benchmarks, tangible evidence. Be able to support them and demonstrate why they are correct for this problem. Drop them when someone else's strong opinion is better suited for the problem based on the data they brought to the table. When we all operate this, we all improve each other as engineers, which is how a team should function.

items.title: Measure before claiming
items.description: If you aren't able to ground what you are saying in data, there's a great likelihood there's something better you could be saying.

items.title: Prefer deterministic systems before inference
items.description: I use models where ambiguity requires them. If a parser, protocol, query, or state machine can produce the fact, I would rather make the fact reproducible. Prefer reproducible deterministic systems, always. Use model inference where needed to produce patterns within that deterministically populated data, that may not be attainable otherwise.

items.title: Abstractions justify their cost
items.description: An abstraction should remove a recurring burden or enforce a valuable constraint. A small simple system is almost inarguably the desired state of all software systems, it's just not the pragmatic state of some. Don't abstract away simplicity for something complex, even if there is elegance in the complexity. At some point, you choose to be an engineer, not an artist.

items.title: Operational quality is architecture
items.description: Accessibility, performance, observability, reversibility, and release behavior belong in the roadmap from day one, and never thought of as a fast follow.

items.title: Follow the problem across boundaries
items.description: Useful systems rarely respect frontend, backend, infrastructure, or native labels. Become an expert at problem solving and at the craft of software, and solve problems wherever they hide.

elsewhere.title: Elsewhere
paragraphs: When I'm not furiously at a keyboard or laptop, I'm spending time with my wife and our two dogs, Chief and Dumpling, watching the Dallas Cowboys, or maybe playing Fortnite, Call of Duty: Black Ops III, or Cult of the Lamb.
I read avidly about pen-and-paper ciphers, modern encryption, and this has taken me into white hat cybersecurity also.
I am a Pokemon TCG Fan, you can often find me at a local card shop, running Ethan's Typhlosion into the ground, judging/hosting a league night, or working on AI/Pokemon related projects.

closing.title: I like using software to solve problems, try out new ideas, and improve our lives
